name: Omar Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three injection moulding presses at Halden Plastics, out on the ring road. We make the little plastic bits inside cars, vent housings, clips, the trim around the gear stick. I clock in at six, check the moulds are up to heat, then it's eight hours of pulling parts, trimming flash with a knife, boxing them and keeping an eye on the screens so nothing short-shots. The noise and the smell of hot plastic get into your clothes, and Lina says she can tell what shift I've done by how I smell.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know those machines. Press two has a cough when the hydraulics warm up and I can hear it from the break room. What wears me out is the pay, honestly, and the rotating nights. I've been there seven years and I still have about three hundred in the bank at the end of the month, if I'm lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Every year there's some salesman in a suit walking the floor with the managers, and every year it's the same presses and the same us. I'd probably post something like 'the robots aren't coming, but the pay rise still isn't either.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays exactly as tight as it is now. Which is a relief and a kick in the teeth at the same time. AI wasn't my problem in the first place, the wages were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep going to the union meetings with Rita, our steward, because the next pay round is in March. I'd maybe push harder on the night-shift allowance, since the company wouldn't have the robot excuse anymore. Nothing else changes, I don't have spare money to change anything with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief. A bit flat, too, because nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI wasn't the problem in the first place. What is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who gets the money. Halden got bought two years ago by a group with a name like a bank, and since then they've cut the canteen hours and frozen the bonus. If AI flops, they'll find some other reason to squeeze us. That's what I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you most like to stop worrying about, if anything got easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan. It's an eleven-year-old hatchback and I owe more on it than it's worth, but there's no bus to the ring road before seven. If that was paid off, I could breathe a bit.

S0.say: I'd tell people I always said the robot talk was mostly sales pitch. I'd joke online that the robots aren't coming, but neither is the pay rise.
S0.think: My life stays as tight as it is now, which is a relief and also a letdown. AI was never the real problem for me; low wages and the new owners were.
S0.do: Keeps working his shifts on the presses and keeps attending union meetings ahead of the March pay round. Pushes for a better night-shift allowance now the company can't point to automation.
S0.feel: Relieved, but flat, because nothing improves either.
S0.quote: It means my life stays exactly as tight as it is now. Which is a relief and a kick in the teeth at the same time.
S0.fieldNote: Omar frames everything through pay and ownership, not technology. He sounded more angry about the new owners than worried about AI. The car loan he can't escape because there's no early bus came up unprompted and seems to sit on him every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need it in writing. If they bring in robot arms to pull parts off the presses, we want a deal on who stays and who gets trained, before the first one's bolted down. Online I'd share the union stuff, the petitions, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be one of the first to go. Pulling parts and trimming flash is exactly the job a robot arm does, and I've already seen one at a trade video Bogdan showed me. I'm average at this, I'm not the setter who fixes the moulds, I'm the guy who stands there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the union committee, properly, not just turn up. I'd want a no-redundancy agreement or at least a fair payout, and I'd ask Lina if we could cut the streaming and the takeaways to put fifty a week aside. I wouldn't go do some coding course, that's not me, and I'd be no good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like when the manager calls your name over the tannoy and you don't know why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't retrain. If the company paid for a course, say in robot maintenance, would that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if Bogdan did it with me. On my own, sitting in a classroom with screens, I'd freeze. I left school because of classrooms. I know that sounds stubborn, and it probably is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where else could you go if Halden cut jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the meat plant in the next town and that's about it. Forty minutes each way, worse money, and they're automating too from what I hear. So I'd be fighting to keep this one rather than looking for another.

S1.say: He'd say workers need a written deal before any robot arm is installed, covering who stays and who gets trained. Online he'd share union petitions and campaign material.
S1.think: He believes his role, pulling parts and trimming, is exactly what a robot arm would take first. He sees himself as average and easy to replace, not like the setter who fixes the moulds.
S1.do: Joins the union committee and pushes for a no-redundancy agreement or a fair payout. Cuts streaming and takeaways with Lina to put about fifty a week aside, while refusing to start a technical course on his own.
S1.feel: A tight chest, like being called to the office without knowing why.
S1.quote: I'm average at this, I'm not the setter who fixes the moulds, I'm the guy who stands there.
S1.fieldNote: Omar is clear-eyed about his own exposure and does not flatter himself. His answer to every threat is collective, never individual. The only crack in his refusal to retrain was the idea of doing it alongside his lunch mate Bogdan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the bosses' dream and our nightmare, and that the government has to step in now, not after. Online I'd be loud. Tax the robots, pay people, something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished in a year. There'd be no Halden as I know it, just a dark building where the lights stay off. And I've got three hundred in the bank and a car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and every protest in the city, I'd sign up for whatever benefits exist before the queue gets huge. Lina and I would probably have to give up the flat and move in with her mum, who has a spare room above the shop. I'd sell the car the day I lost the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't really have a plan, I have reactions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what's the one thing you'd do this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ring my mum. She'd hear it from me, not the news. Then I'd ask Rita what the union can actually do in two years, because I suspect the answer is not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bogdan. He's fifty-six, he's been at Halden since it opened, and he can't read the screens without his glasses. He's the one who taught me which press coughs. He'd have nowhere.

S2.say: He'd call it the bosses' dream and workers' nightmare and demand that government act immediately. Online he'd push hard for taxing robots and paying people directly.
S2.think: He expects his job and the plant as he knows it to be gone within a year. With about three hundred saved and a car loan, he sees no cushion at all.
S2.do: Attends every union meeting and protest and signs up for benefits early. Plans to sell the car once he loses the job and move with Lina into her mother's spare room above the shop.
S2.feel: Like the floor has gone; he has reactions, not a plan.
S2.quote: There'd be no Halden as I know it, just a dark building where the lights stay off. And I've got three hundred in the bank and a car loan.
S2.fieldNote: This was the first time Omar's voice dropped. He admitted he has 'reactions, not a plan', which felt very honest. His worry quickly went to Bogdan, an older colleague, more than to himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse. Unions, councils, the government, they all need to be ready with a plan for people like us. I'd be on that at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see it coming and not enough to do anything about it, for me. I'm not going to become a software person by thirty-two. So I think it buys the bosses time more than it buys me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try harder to save, really try, maybe pick up Saturday overtime while it still exists and put all of it away. I'd push the union to fight for long notice and a big redundancy pot. And I'd vote for whoever promises a basic income, I'm not shy about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like watching a slow train come down the track while you're tied to it. Less shock than the fast one, more dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years buys the bosses time more than you. What would the bosses do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy the robots slowly, so nobody makes a fuss. One press this year, two the next. By the time we notice, half the floor's gone and the other half is scared to say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lina change in your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about kids, maybe around thirty. In that world we'd probably wait. Her job in the care home might last longer than mine, so she'd be the earner, and I'd have to get used to that.

S3.say: He'd argue five years leaves no excuse for unions, councils and government not to have a plan for workers like him. He'd raise it at every meeting.
S3.think: He believes five years lets him see it coming but is too short for him to change trades. He suspects the time mostly helps employers bring robots in quietly.
S3.do: Takes Saturday overtime while it exists and saves all of it. Pushes the union for long notice and a large redundancy fund, and votes for candidates who back a basic income.
S3.feel: Dread rather than shock, like watching a slow train approach.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to see it coming and not enough to do anything about it, for me.
S3.fieldNote: Omar doesn't see extra time as his time; he sees it as the employer's time. The detail about robots arriving 'one press this year, two the next' showed how he expects change to feel on the floor. He also quietly pushed back plans for children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Shorter weeks, retraining paid properly, a fund for people whose jobs go. That's what I'd be posting and saying in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know I'm the kind of person who uses ten years to put things off. I'd keep thinking there's time, and then it's year eight. So I'm not sure it helps me as much as it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the five-year one, union first. But with ten years I'd maybe do the forklift and warehouse tickets, small things that don't feel like school. And I'd want Lina and me out of debt by the time it lands, so the car loan goes first, then a little pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still heavy. Less like the floor's gone, more like a storm you can see on the horizon every single day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said you'd put things off, but also that you'd do forklift tickets. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, probably. I'd do the forklift one because it's a weekend and a test, I can handle that. The big stuff, changing who I am, I'd keep putting off. That's just being honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be at Halden in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it exists. I'd be thirty-seven. My dad was at the brickworks till it shut and he never really worked again properly. I think about that more than I let on.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift if it's used for shorter weeks, properly paid retraining and a fund for displaced workers. He'd say that in the canteen and online.
S4.think: He admits he tends to put things off and worries he'd waste the decade. He doubts the extra time would help him as much as it should.
S4.do: Prioritises union work, then takes short practical tickets such as forklift licences. Aims to clear the car loan first and build a small savings pot with Lina before AGI arrives.
S4.feel: Heavy, like a storm visible on the horizon every day.
S4.quote: My dad was at the brickworks till it shut and he never really worked again properly. I think about that more than I let on.
S4.fieldNote: With the longest warning, Omar was most self-critical, admitting he'd delay. The story of his father at the brickworks seems to sit under all of his answers. He accepts small, test-based training but resists anything that feels like going back to school.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'd have no money, no time and no other plant to go to. What would help is money straight to people, not a leaflet about online courses, and a law that says if a company replaces you with a machine, it pays into a fund for you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole thing for me. If the robots belonged to all of us, a machine doing my job would be good news. It's only bad news because it's somebody else's machine.

headlineQuote: If the robots belonged to all of us, a machine doing my job would be good news. It's only bad news because it's somebody else's machine.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old press operator at a plastics plant on a ring road, living with his partner Lina, a care home worker, with about three hundred in the bank and a car loan he can't escape. He knows his machines by sound but sees himself as easy to replace. He reads every scenario through pay and ownership, and his answers are always collective: the union, protests, votes for a basic income. He gets steadily more frightened as AGI comes sooner, and with more time he admits he would probably put off the hard changes, thinking of his father who never worked properly after the brickworks closed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no money, no time and no other plant nearby to go to.
whatWouldHelp: Money paid straight to people rather than course leaflets, and a law making companies that replace workers with machines pay into a fund for them.
